Glycaemic endpoints

At week 24 (LOCF), Gla-300 was associated with marked reductions in HbA1c from baseline in the insulin-naive and prior BI groups, regardless of baseline age (Figure 1A) or disease duration (Figure 1B).

Change in HbA1c from baseline to week 24 in the mITT population by prior insulin status and (A) baseline age or (B) baseline disease duration.  Estimated by a general linear model, adjusted for disease duration, baseline HbA1c, FPG and BMI. BI, basal insulin; BMI, body mass index; CI, confidence interval; FPG, fasting plasma glucose; HbA1c, glycated haemoglobin; LSM, least squares mean; mITT, modified intention-to-treat.

In subgroups defined by baseline age, significant HbA1c reductions were observed in participants aged <60 or >=60 years in both the insulin-naive and prior BI groups (Figure 1A). The LSM change in HbA1c from baseline to week 24 was -1.32% (-14.4 mmol/mol) and -1.40% (-15.3 mmol/mol) in insulin-naive participants aged <60 and >=60 years, respectively, and -0.69% (-7.5 mmol/mol) in both age subgroups in the prior BI group. The LSM difference between age subgroups for HbA1c change was -0.09% (-1.0 mmol/mol) in the insulin-naive group and -0.01% (-0.1 mmol/mol) in the prior BI group. Findings from the sensitivity analysis were in line with these results (data not shown).

HbA1c reductions from baseline to week 24 were also significant across subgroups defined by baseline disease duration (Figure 1B). The LSM change in HbA1c from baseline to week 24 ranged from -1.02% (-11.1 mmol/mol) in the >=10 years subgroup to -1.55% (-16.9 mmol/mol) in the >=5 to <10 years subgroup in the insulin-naive group and from -0.55% (-6.0 mmol/mol) in the >=10 to <15 years subgroup to -0.76% (-8.3 mmol/mol) in the <10 years subgroup in the prior BI group. One exception was among insulin-naive participants, where HbA1c reductions were smaller in the >=10 versus <5 years' disease duration subgroup (LSM difference 0.40% [4.4 mmol/mol]; p = 0.030). Sensitivity analysis HbA1c results were in line with the findings of the main analysis (data not shown), with the exception of the comparison between the >=10 to <15 years and <10 years disease duration subgroups in the prior BI group, where the LSM difference reached statistical significance (0.22; 95% CI 0.01, 0.43; p = 0.038).

The proportion of participants who achieved HbA1c <7.0% (<53 mmol/mol) at week 24 ranged from 22.5% to 30.8% and from 19.5% to 40.7% across the subgroups defined by baseline age (Table 3) and disease duration (Table 4), respectively. Reductions from baseline in FPG and average 7-point SMBG at week 24 were generally similar across all age and disease duration subgroups in insulin-naive participants and in most subgroups among participants in the prior BI group. However, exceptions to this were observed in the prior BI group, where FPG reductions were greater in participants aged >=60 versus <60 years (LSM difference -0.55 mmol/L; p = 0.041), and the average 7-point SMBG reductions were smaller in patients with >=10 to <15 versus <10 years' disease duration (LSM difference 0.59 mmol/L; p = 0.020).

Daily insulin dose

The daily insulin dose increased from baseline to week 24 across all subgroups defined by baseline age (Table S1) and disease duration (Table S2). In insulin-naive participants aged <60 and >=60 years, the LSM change in insulin dose at week 24 was 10.08 U (0.13 U/kg) and 9.21 U (0.13 U/kg), respectively. In the prior BI group, the LSM change in insulin dose at week 24 was 9.05 U (0.12 U/kg) and 8.12 U (0.11 U/kg) in the respective age subgroups. Across subgroups defined by baseline disease duration, the LSM change in insulin dose ranged from 8.84 to 11.45 U (0.11 to 0.15 U/kg) in the insulin-naive group and 7.71-9.10 U (0.11-0.13 U/kg) in the prior BI group.
Hypoglycaemia

The incidence and event rates of any hypoglycaemia (i.e., severe hypoglycaemia, confirmed hypoglycaemia with BG <=3.9 or <3.0 mmol/L or documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia with BG <=3.9 or <3.0 mmol/L) were generally similar across all subgroups defined by baseline age (36.7%-50.8% [2.87-4.13 per PY]; Table S3) and disease duration (38.3%-48.0% [2.82-4.53 per PY]; Table S4). However, exceptions to this were observed in the disease duration subgroups. The event rate of confirmed hypoglycaemia (BG <3.0 mmol/L) was lower in insulin-naive participants with >=5 to <10 versus <5 years' duration (RR 0.27; p = 0.020). The event rate of documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia (BG <=3.9 mmol/L) was higher in insulin-naive participants with >=5 to <10 years' (RR 1.78; p = 0.041) or >=10 years' (RR 2.95; p < 0.001) versus <5 years' duration, and lower in prior BI participants with >=15 versus <10 years' duration (RR 0.62; p = 0.035). Over the 24-week study period, severe hypoglycaemia was only reported in three participants aged >=60 years and two participants with >=15 years' duration; all cases of severe hypoglycaemia were from the prior BI group.
Body weight

Gla-300 was associated with minimal changes in body weight from baseline to week 24 across all subgroups defined by baseline age (Table S5) and disease duration (Table S6). Among participants in the prior BI group with >=15 years' disease duration, this change in body weight was significantly different from those with <10 years' disease duration (LSM difference -0.97 kg; p = 0.044). Similar changes in body weight were observed in all other subgroups.
Treatment satisfaction

Treatment satisfaction increased from baseline to week 24, as demonstrated by increases in DTSQ total score and decreases in DTSQ item 2 (perception of hyperglycaemia) and item 3 (perception of hypoglycaemia) scores. Similar increases in DTSQ total score were observed across all subgroups defined by age, with insulin-naive participants aged <60 and >=60 years having LSM increases of 2.30 and 2.36, respectively, and participants in the prior BI group having LSM increases of 2.42 and 2.31 in the respective age subgroups (Table S7). In the prior BI group, the DTSQ item 3 score showed smaller reductions among participants aged >=60 versus <60 years (LSM difference 0.27; p = 0.042); all other reductions in the DTSQ item 2 and item 3 scores were similar across the age subgroups. The increase in DTSQ score was also similar across all disease duration subgroups, with the LSM increases of 1.94-2.78 in the insulin-naive group and 2.25-2.45 in the prior BI group (Table S8). A greater reduction in the DTSQ item 3 score was observed among participants in the prior BI group with >=15 versus <10 years' disease duration (LSM difference -0.35; p = 0.026); all other reductions in the DTSQ item 2 and item 3 scores were similar across the disease duration subgroups.
DISCUSSION

The findings of this post-hoc analysis of the INITIATION study suggest that Gla-300 provides improvements in glycaemic control and is well tolerated in people with suboptimally controlled T2D in China, regardless of baseline age and T2D disease duration. In this analysis, Gla-300 provided clinically meaningful improvements in glycaemic control over 24 weeks' treatment in all study participants, including older individuals (aged >=60 years) and those with long-standing disease duration (>=10 or >=15 years). These results are in line with the findings of previous RCTs and real-world studies of Gla-300 in older individuals with T2D, although it should be noted that the age-group cutoff for these prior analyses was 65 years, whereas the current analysis used an age-group cutoff of 60 years as the large majority of individuals with T2D in China are aged >=60 years, and a 60-year age threshold is more representative of China's older population. Similar HbA1c reductions with Gla-300 versus Gla-100 over 26 weeks (or 6 months) were previously reported among participants with T2D aged >=65 years in the SENIOR study and in a patient-level meta-analyses of pooled data from the global EDITION studies. A subanalysis of the BRIGHT study also reported similar glycaemic efficacy with Gla-300 versus insulin degludec 100 U/mL over 24 weeks in participants aged <65 and >=65 years, with Gla-300 providing greater HbA1c reductions in those aged >=75 years. In the real-world DELIVER 3 study, Gla-300 was associated with similar or better glycaemic efficacy compared with first-generation BIs (i.e., Gla-100 or insulin detemir) in older people (aged >=65 years) with T2D after switching from prior BI therapy. Similarly, a multicentre observational study of individuals with T2D who switched from neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin to Gla-300 reported similar glycaemic efficacy in older (>=65 years) and younger (<65 years) individuals.

Among participants with prior BI therapy in this analysis, Gla-300 provided glycaemic benefits regardless of T2D disease duration. Similarly, a patient-level meta-analysis of pooled EDITION data found that Gla-300 had comparable glycaemic control to that of Gla-100, regardless of the duration of prior BI therapy. Furthermore, the REALI European study reported that Gla-300 improved HbA1c reductions over 24 weeks in insulin-naive individuals with T2D, regardless of disease duration (<8 or >=8 years). In contrast, the previous observational study of individuals switching from NPH insulin to Gla-300 reported greater HbA1c reductions in those with shorter (<=13 years) versus longer (>13 years) disease duration. Taken together, these data suggests that individuals with long-standing, suboptimally controlled T2D on other BI therapy may benefit from switching to Gla-300.

In this analysis, insulin-naive participants with longer T2D disease duration (>=10 years) had smaller HbA1c reductions than those with shorter disease duration (<5 years), while reductions in FPG and average 7-point SMBG were similar across disease duration subgroups. This emphasises the importance of early initiation of BI and avoiding clinical inertia in insulin-naive individuals with suboptimally controlled T2D. Indeed, evidence from the post-trial monitoring of the 20-year United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) and a retrospective cohort study from Japan indicate that early initiation of insulin, in particular second-generation BIs, may provide long-term organ protection that helps to preserve beta-cell function and prevent diabetic complications.

The incidence and event rates of hypoglycaemia with Gla-300 in this analysis were low and generally similar regardless of age or T2D disease duration. Of note, severe hypoglycaemia was observed only in the prior BI group among three participants aged >=60 years and two with >=15 years' T2D duration (both of whom were aged >=60 years). In these individuals, the combined impact of advanced age and prolonged disease duration most likely led to impaired beta-cell function (i.e., reduced capacity to rapidly secrete insulin in response to blood glucose fluctuations), thereby causing greater blood glucose variability and an increased risk of severe hypoglycaemia. In contrast with our findings, a study in individuals who switched from NPH insulin to Gla-300 reported a greater reduction in the incidence of hypoglycaemia among individuals aged >=65 versus <65 years. This previous observational study in individuals switching from prior NPH insulin also reported a lower hypoglycaemia event rate with Gla-300 in those with >13 years' disease duration. Consistent with the findings of the current analysis, the previous real-world REALI study reported low incidence and event rates for symptomatic and severe hypoglycaemia with Gla-300 in insulin-naive individuals, regardless of age (<50, 50-59, 60-69, 70-79 and >=80 years) or disease duration (<8 or >=8 years).

The pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic profile of Gla-300 is more stable than that of Gla-100, which may have contributed to the low incidence of hypoglycaemia with Gla-300 in older individuals. The once-daily dosing schedule of Gla-300 may also help to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia, particularly as simplified insulin regimens are recommended in older individuals with T2D to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia. Given that China has the largest population of older adults with T2D in the world, and that many of these individuals will require insulin therapy as disease progresses, Gla-300 may offer clinically relevant benefits to this older population.

In addition to improvements in glycaemic control and low risk of hypoglycaemia, Gla-300 was associated with improvements in treatment satisfaction, as reflected by DTSQ scores, across all baseline age and disease duration subgroups. Similarly, the previous real-world TRANSITION2 study in France reported a 20% improvement in DTSQ scores among 136 individuals who switched from prior BI therapy to Gla-300 (mean age 61.7 years; mean disease duration 14.6 years). The global ATOS PRO study has also reported real-world improvements in DTSQ scores over 12 months among 3801 insulin-naive individuals with T2D who initiated Gla-300 treatment, with 76% of participants showing meaningful DTSQs improvement (DTSQs total score improvement of >=4 points) at month 12. Improvements in patient-reported treatment satisfaction, as measured by the DTSQ, have been associated with enhanced treatment adherence and may lead to improved long-term glycaemic control. Therefore, improved treatment satisfaction with Gla-300 may be expected to result in better treatment adherence and consequently glycaemic control in Chinese individuals with T2D.

The main strength of this post-hoc analysis is that it is the first study to evaluate the glycaemic control and safety of Gla-300 in older individuals and those with long-standing T2D in China, including both insulin-naive individuals and those switching from prior BI therapy. The limitations of this analysis include those related to the lack of a control group in the primary study and the lack of prespecified subgroup analyses with sufficient statistical power due to small sample sizes, which can limit the generalisability of the results. However, the estimation of LSM differences between subgroups with corresponding 95% CIs allowed for exploratory comparison of treatment outcomes with Gla-300 between subgroups.

In conclusion, Gla-300 was associated with sustained glycaemic control across all ages and T2D disease durations in Chinese people with T2D, including older individuals and those with long-standing disease, with a low hypoglycaemia risk. Thus, Gla-300 may be a suitable treatment option for T2D management in older individuals and those with long-standing disease in China.

passages.text: Enhanced colorectal gland segmentation through multi-scale attention and contextual feature fusion

Histological image segmentation of colorectal cancer plays a crucial role in reliable cancer grading, prognosis evaluation, and treatment planning. Nevertheless, existing automated approaches often struggle due to fine-grained glandular structures, staining variations, acquisition differences across scanners and highly heterogeneous tissue morphology. To address these challenges, we propose MAC-Net, an enhanced deep learning model that integrates multi-scale feature fusion with attention-guided contextual decoding to achieve precise gland segmentation across diverse tumor differentiation stages. MAC-Net retains fine structural information by channel-wise attention, enhances learning of discriminative features by the increased number of enriched encoder-decoder lateral connections, and the global contextual information, by means of multi-scale spatial pooling at the bottleneck. To determine the generalizability of the model, we trained the model on the EBHI-Seg data (2228 images) and cross-validated it on the GIaS data (165 images). MAC-Net achieved 95.08% Dice, 90.92% IoU, 95.83% Precision, and 95.65% Recall, outperforming existing architectures. Furthermore, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping visualization and uncertainty analysis enhance interpretability, provides deeper insight on model's transparent behavior and supports reliable clinical decision-making in the field of digital pathology.
Introduction

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a fast-growing cancerous disease globally, as it takes the second position in the global mortality rate. CRC in India has been posting a gradual, steady rise of between 2%-3% in incidence over the past two decades, with a survival rate markedly lower than that in developed countries. Traditionally, healthcare professionals rely on labor-intensive manual histopathological analysis for detection and classification, which informs treatment strategies. Nevertheless, manual analysis is prone to misdiagnosis due to subjectivity, inter-observer variability, and the complexity of human tissue structures.The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed the paradigm of pathology by enabling precise diagnoses, simplifying clinical work, and customizing treatment. The emergence of Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) has given greater attention to digital pathology. The systematic pathological examination of tissue samples is still the gold standard of CRC diagnosis, but AI may be used to aid pathologists in their work, such as tissue segmentation, subtyping of cancer, prediction of cancer margins, and survival analysis. ML/DL-based approaches can be more effective and reliable than the manual ones as they enable faster reporting and enhance objectivity in measurement.

Manual gland segmentation is a highly time-consuming and subjective process that requires the expertise of well-trained pathologists. This explains why automated approaches are necessary to aid cancer diagnosis. However, it is still difficult to develop segmentation models that are robust across all the grades of CRC. The ML approaches are useful in preliminary segmentation and classification, but in cases of severe tissue variation and textual inequality, they fail. These complexities, however, can be very well expressed in the DL models.Among these, U-Net has been one of the well-known biomedical segmentation models. Its encoder-decoder structure with skip connections maintains both global context and fine-scale spatial data that is important in the segmentation of complex structures such as glands and tumorous areas.

The challenges associated with histopathological images of CRC include intricate tissue structure, morphological deviations, and slight disparities among tissue classes. The conventional U-Net finds difficulty in reflecting these complex patterns because its skip connections are limited in combining low-level spatial and high-level semantic features. Therefore, the U-Net results in poor performance on class imbalance segmentation. Later studies added UNet++ and VNet, which use nested and dense skip connections to enhance localization, yet they are still weak at global context. Attention UNet increases the saliency of features via attention gates and has difficulty with variability in multi-resolution due to variations in lesion size and shape. In a bid to address these shortcomings, hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models have been employed, and these have resulted in good segmentation in more complex tissue environments. Nevertheless, they have high computational overhead due to their greater complexity in architecture, which impedes practical deployment. Several challenges to effective segmentation of colorectal histopathology images have thus been identified as the need to tackle the existence of varying gland sizes, intra-class variation, delicate inter-tissue variations, and staining artifacts.
MAC-Net model for enhanced colorectal histopathological segmentation.

Our proposed MAC-Net is frameworked with a system of information fusion among various spatial resolutions to delineate the boundaries of glands and tumors in the most accurate way. It improves representation of features by dynamically exploiting informative areas and dropping irrelevant or noisy features, and is resistant to background clutter and staining aliasing. MAC-Net processes multiple scales of semantic cues to provide the larger context, which allows the distinction between precancerous and malignant tissues. Transformer-augmented and prior attention-based models emphasize the importance of enriched context, although most of them focus on one or two of them independently. MAC-Net integrates the spatial, channel-level, and contextual features in a single encoder-decoder (U-Net) system as its backbone and optimizes hierarchy to offer robust features in segmentation among different stages of CRC. Figure 1 gives a comprehensive overview of the entire framework.

Our proposed framework, MAC-Net, a gland segmentation system for colorectal cancer histopathology images, is a versatile system that combines better feature association, dynamic attention, and multi-scale context modelling.

A context-capturing module is introduced at the core of the network to consolidate the information across multiple scales, while on the other hand, the attention mechanisms fine-tune features before fusion in the reconstruction path.
We introduce a tailored loss function - an integration of Dice, Focal, and Edge losses to enhance the accuracy of the boundaries and to counter the imbalance existing among the classes trained.
Grad-CAM facilitates model transparency and interpretability by visualizing influential regions of decision-making in segmentation.
Monte Carlo Dropout is employed to quantify prediction uncertainty, enabling identification of low-confidence cases that may require expert review.
The generalizability of MAC-Net is validated through cross-dataset testing on the GIaS dataset, demonstrating robustness to unseen histopathological data with varying characteristics.
The major contributions of this work are summarized as follows,
Related works

This section reviews existing approaches in CRC histopathological segmentation, including CNN-based U-Net models, their variants, attention-enhanced models, and hybrid frameworks, with additional focus on emerging transformer-based techniques. We also highlight contributions utilizing self-supervised and multi-task learning strategies.
CNN and U-Net variants

Sengupta et al. conducted a comparative study to evaluate the performance of six CNN-based segmentation models - namely, U-Net, Attention U-Net, and U-Net with backbone networks including ResNet50, MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB0, and DenseNet121 for gland segmentation in histopathological images. Their finding indicated that the U-Net with DenseNet121 and ResNet50 backbones achieved superior segmentation accuracy compared to the other variants. Liyu et al. introduced the EBHI-Seg dataset for analysis of CRC at various stages - early to advanced. They evaluated a host of ML and DL models on the dataset. The precision of the ML methods reached up to 70%, whereas the DL methods reached a much higher level (90%).
Attention enhanced and hybrid models

Although the U-Net is a very successful model in extracting local features, it does not always provide the larger global context. To overcome this shortcoming, the U-Net is coupled with an Efficient Multi-scale Attention (EMA) module. This EMA-Swin U-Net model allows the presence of robust feature representation across tissue scales. Similarly, the Dynamic Mixture of Convolutions U-Net (DMoC-UNet), uses adaptive expert pathways that dynamically adapt to structural variations, improving segmentation of heterogeneous lesion areas.
Transformer based models

Although the number of reported applications is low, recent research has proven the increasing interest in Transformer-based models, supported by their ability to process spatially heterogeneous histopathological images.. CervixFormer is a Swin Transformer-based classification framework showing excellent performance in classifying malignant cells, with Grad-CAM visualizations that were used to interpret the classified images. The models leverage a self-attention mechanism to obtain long-range dependencies in images, which is beneficial to task segmenting large and spatially intricate structures in Whole Slide Images (WSI). Minimal Information Loss Dilated Network (MILD-Net) is a fully convolutional network that preserves significant information by reintroducing the original image and atrous spatial pyramid pooling, thereby discretionary the extraction of features on multi-scale level. MILD-Net uses random transformations at test time in order to deal with prediction uncertainty, and this improves segmentation and highlights ambiguous regions.
Multi-task and self-supervised learning

In addition to the supervised methods, self-supervised learning (SSL) has been considered to utilise unlabeled CRC data. The multi-resolution SSL framework involves context-target fusion and masked jigsaw tasks modules, to promote multi-resolution feature learning and hence leading to the improvement of segmentation of cancer datasets over current approaches in WSI. Graham et al applied a multi-task learning (MTL) framework for the simultaneous segmentation and classification of nuclei, glands, lumina, and various tissue regions in in diagnosing CRC. A tailored sampling technique and shared features of the framework enabled them to learn from multiple datasets.
Methodology

This section presents the methodology adopted for developing the MAC-Net framework for gland segmentation in CRC histopathological images. MAC-Net uses channel-wise attention, multi-scale feature fusion, and contextual information aggregation implied with an encoder-decoder architecture in order to increase the precision of segmentation among all stages of cancer and also glandular structures. Each module is discussed in detail in the upcoming subsections. The systematic architecture of the proposed model is illustrated in Fig. 2.
MAC-Net architecture
MAC-Net architecture highlighting multi-scale feature aggregation and contextual-attention fusion.

The input of the model is a normalized histopathological image, which is 256256 pixels (px) with 3 color channels. To extract semantic and spatial features, the encoder path has four convolutional blocks, each with two convolutional layers, then dropout, and max pooling. Each encoder block is followed by a feature enhancement attention module, which is also used in the skip connections, learning to refine the features before combining them with the decoder in order to provide rich context representations. A multi-scale feature extraction unit is present at the bottleneck, which takes in contextual information with pooled representation at various spatial levels, which are produced by the use of convolution and upsampling operations. The decoder also assumes a hierarchical architecture with every upsampling stage incorporating improved encoder characteristics through lateral skip connections. And these concatenated features are aimed at and polished with convolution layers. MAC-Net is trained by a hybrid loss that uses the Dice loss, Focal loss, and Edge loss. The architecture guarantees cluster-accurate region segmentation, resistance to class imbalance, and delineation of the boundaries correctly.
Hierarchical feature extraction

The MAC-Net encoder is designed as a hierarchical feature extractor, which has four levels of downsampling to extract characteristic features of colorectal histopathology images at various levels of abstraction. The encoder includes four convolutional blocks, each consisting of two convolutional layers with kernel size 33, ReLU activation, and same padding, followed by a Dropout layer to regularize learning. The number of filters doubles at each subsequent level starting from 32, 64, 128, and 256. A MaxPooling2D operation with a 22 window and stride 2 is applied only after the first three blocks to increase the receptive field and reduce spatial dimensions.

The final convolutional block processes the output of  through two Conv2D layers with 256 filters and a dropout rate of 0.2, without further pooling. This generates a 44 high-level semantic representation, which is passed to a multi-scale context aggregation module. The absence of pooling in this final stage allows the network to retain the highest semantic abstraction while preserving fine spatial granularity, an important factor for enhancing boundary-level segmentation during decoding.
Contextual feature aggregation

To enhance the network for modeling long-range dependencies and global structures across variable-sized tissue regions, the deepest encoder output is passed through a multi-scale context aggregation module. This module performs average pooling at multiple granularities (e.g., 22 and 44) on the encoded feature map , followed by dimensionality reduction using 11 convolutions, and spatial upsampling to the original size via bilinear interpolation. The original feature map and the upsampled features from all scales are concatenated along the channel dimensions to form an enhanced feature representation as defined below,The fusion yields , where . By integrating features across multiple scales, this representation strengthens the network's robustness in differentiating similar textured regions, such as overlapping glands or ill-defined tumor margins. This context-enriched output then acts as the input to the decoder.
Decoder with multi-scale attention fusion

Segmentation map is progressively reconstructed in the decoder by combining context-enhanced features from the encoder and upsampled decoder outputs through lateral skip connections. These weights recalibrate the original feature map as below,This recalibration sharpens focus on diagnostically relevant structures such as gland borders, epithelial layers, and tumor boundaries. These enriched features from encoder levels  are merged with decoder outputs to guide spatially-aware reconstruction.
Output segmentation layer

After feature refinement across all decoder stages, the final output feature map of size 25625632 is processed by a 11 convolution layer followed by a sigmoid activation to generate a binary segmentation mask. The convolutional layer feature is then processed through the sigmoid activation function to produce a probability map as below,where  is the output feature map from the decoder, and  denotes a convolution with kernel size 11.  is the projected single-channel feature map,  is the pixel value at location (i, j) in ,  denotes the sigmoid function, and  represents the predicted probability that pixel (i, j) belongs to the glandular region.

Representing the confidence that a given pixel belongs to the glandular region, the process ensures that each probability value lies within the range [0,1]. A threshold of 0.5 is applied to convert the probability map into a binary segmentation mask as below,where  denotes the binary classification of each pixel, with 1 indicating gland and 0 indicating background.  is the final binary segmentation map.
Combined loss function

We propose , a hybrid loss function which is a weighted combination of Focal Loss, Dice Loss, and Edge Loss. Each component targets a specific limitation in medical image segmentation such as class imbalance, small structure sensitivity, and boundary precision. The final model is trained by minimizing this composite loss function using backpropagation with the Adam optimizer. The Dice Loss measures  overlap with , the ground truth mask. This loss addresses class imbalance. Dice loss promotes overlap and equally avoids under- and over-segmentation, which is critical for small or sparse gland regions.The Focal Loss is used to reduce the influence of pixels that were correctly predicted and place more focus on the hard-to-classify pixels near gland boundaries or uncertain regions. Such a loss actively scales down the cross-entropy loss to focus more on misclassified pixels and enhances generalization in cases of extreme imbalance between classes.The Edge Loss promotes convergence between the expected and ground truth bounds with the application of gradient-based edge detection with Sobel filters. This loss term punishes disparities in the sharpness of edges and leads to clearer glandular edges as described below,The hybrid loss is then defined as below:In this work,  were assigned equal importance, with each set to 0.3. The residual weight of 0.1 was kept for regularization or minor adjustments if required. This balanced setup helps the model improve region accuracy, address class imbalance, and sharpen boundaries, thereby enabling more reliable gland segmentation.
Grad-CAM based explainability

To improve interpretability of the proposed MAC-Net model, Grad-CAM was applied to visualize spatial regions that contribute to the model's decision. In binary segmentation, Grad-CAM was computed by averaging the predicted output prior to backpropagating the gradients to the final convolution layer. Uncertainty estimation

To estimate the model-related (epistemic) uncertainty in segmentation outputs, we employed Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout during inference. Dropout layers, usually disabled during inference, were kept active to introduce randomness in predictions. This enabled the model to produce multiple outputs per input, allowing uncertainty estimation through variability measurement across predictions. For each test image, the model performed  stochastic forward passes, generating multiple segmentation outputs . The mean of these predictions was regarded as the final segmentation result, as expressed below:where  represents the predicted probability map from the -th forward pass and  is the number of stochastic passes. Pixel-wise variance across outputs was computed to represent epistemic uncertainty, as shown below:where  is the prediction from the -th pass and  is the mean prediction across all passes. The uncertainty approach was implemented using a TensorFlow inference loop, ensuring dropout remained active at test time. The resulting variance map highlights areas where the model is less certain, while image-wise mean variance was used as an overall uncertainty score.
Experiment and results
In this section, we provide a comprehensive overview of the experimental setup and present the evaluation results demonstrating the performance of MAC-Net.
Dataset description
Sample images from EBHI-Seg and GIaS dataset.

The investigation in this work adopted the publicly available EBHI-Seg dataset, which consists of 4,452 histopathological images: 2,226 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained colon tissue images and 2,226 corresponding ground truth segmentation masks. TThe images were taken under 400X magnification with Nissan Olympus microscope and stored in 256256 pixels in portable network graphics (PNG) format. The data set was carefully filtered with ethical guidance by highly qualified pathologists in the Cancer Hospital of China Medical University, Shenyang, Liaoning, China, and was released online. EBHI-Seg is unique in the sense that it includes six annotated classes of colorectal tissues consisting of diverse tumor stages such as normal, polyp, low-grade, and high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia (IN), serrated adenoma, and adenocarcinoma. It gives a detailed description of the progressive stages of CRC presented in terms of training, validation, and test sets. This renders the dataset applicable in training and evaluating semantic segmentation networks such as MAC-Net in a clinically meaningful setting. Generalizability of MAC-Net was also tested on the GIaS dataset, comprising 165 colon histological image samples of benign or malignant cancer, and expert-labeled gland segmentation masks. The GIaS images are characterized by high inter-subject variability in the distribution of the stain and structure of the tissue, and varied magnifications, as well as a resolution of about 0.465 microm/ pixel. This cross-dataset validation justifies the strength of MAC-Net in a variety of clinical imaging settings. Figure 3 demonstrate a sample of the respective dataset (EBHI-Seg and GIaS).
Experimental details

MAC-Net has been trained on Google Colab with a Tesla T4 16GB VRAM with the help of TensorFlow 2.12.0. The model was trained using a batch size of 10 and 100 epochs with the input size set at 2562563. All the images and masks were scaled to 256 x 256 pixels, and the min-max scaling was used to normalize to the range [0,1]. A fixed random seed ensured consistent augmentation across training epochs. To ensure fair and reproducible comparison and division of the dataset, the benchmark was used to split the EBHI-Seg dataset into training, validation, and test sets in a 4:4:2 ratio. A large enough validation set minimizes chances of overfitting, which can happen with smaller splits (e.g., 8:1:1). Monitor validation performance and save the best-performing model were done by early stopping (patience =10,verbose=1), learning rate reduction on plateau (factor = 0.1, patience = 5, minimum learning rate = 1e-4), and model checkpointing.

Dice Score, Precision, Recall, Intersection-over-Union (IoU), and Conformity Coefficient were used to measure performance of the model. Interpretability was done with Grad-CAM visualizations and inference with Monte Carlo Dropout to produce multifold predictions for inference of both the mean and variance-based uncertainty maps.
Evaluation metrics

To internally validate, the EBHI-Seg data were divided into training, validation, and test subsets in a 4:4:2 proportion, ensuring balanced representation across all six CRC classes. The training and validation sets each contained 890 images, while the test set had 446 images. This stratified split enabled fair and consistent evaluation. Cross-dataset generalizability was evaluated using the GIaS dataset as an external test set. The evaluation metrics used were Dice Score, Precision, Recall, IoU, and Conformity Coefficient, as defined in the EBHI-Seg benchmark. Their mathematical definitions are given as follows:Here,  represents the predicted probability at pixel i and  represents the ground truth at pixel i.  is a small constant (e.g., ) to avoid division by zero. Dice and IoU measure overlap between predicted and actual regions; Precision and Recall assess missing or extra regions, and the Conformity Coefficient evaluates overall prediction accuracy against the ground truth.

Cross dataset testing on GIaS dataset
MAC-Net model training and validation performance metrics over epochs.

In order to test the generalizability of MAC-Net, we tested the model in the GIaS dataset, which contains 165 histopathological images and their associated ground truth annotations. GIaS images were initially pre-processed to deal with high inter-subject variation, with processes such as normalization, contrast enhancement, and noise elimination. The trained MAC-Net model, which was trained on the weights of the EBHI-Seg, was used to directly infer GIaS images. The model achieved 80.1% accuracy, 81.0% Dice score, 70.1% IoU, 80.25% precision, 85.7% recall, and 80.9% conformity coefficient. Figure 6 depicts a sample from segmentation produced on the GIaS dataset.

Figure 7 shows a performance comparison between MAC-Net on EBHI-Seg and the GIaS data. Even though it was trained on EBHI-Seg only, it generalized moderately at GIaS with a total performance of around 80%. Models that are trained and tested on GIaS normally achieve a performance of 70-85%. The observed performance drop can be explained by the fact that EBHI-Seg has defined categories of cancer and homogenous staining properties, whereas GIaS has more significant variability in tissue appearance, structure, and distribution of stains. MAC-Net was also superior in EBHI-Seg compared to DMoC-UNet. DMoC-UNet, which was trained using 85 GIaS images and tested using 80 images, achieved an average accuracy of 85%. By comparison, the MAC-Net achieves an accuracy of 80% without any pre-training or fine-tuning on GIaS, which suggests that it did experience some cross-dataset generalization even with the data shift. Compared to the model mentioned above, MAC-Net exhibited competitive flexibility on unseen GIaS samples.
Model output comparison: trained vs. external dataset.

To infer from the Segmentation outputs from the GIaS dataset in terms to highlight best, average, and worst-case performance scenarios. The best case (Dice = 0.96) shows a great match between prediction and ground truth, with small differences in the boundaries. There is a good agreement in the average case (Dice = 0.83); the contours of the fine-scale glands are not entirely well-conserved in structure. The worst scenario (Dice = 0.3014) was when there were dense stromal patterns and severe distortion thereof, which posed a great challenge. Notably, high recall values ( 95%) implying that MAC-Net would minimize the number of false negatives of the glandular structures in this data, which is desirable in terms of a diagnostic perspective.

To the best of our knowledge, EBHI-Seg and GlaS are the only publicly accessible colorectal gland segmentation datasets in histopathology, and both were used for quantitative evaluation in this work. To further assess the generalizability of MAC-Net beyond colorectal tissue, we additionally conducted a small-scale cross-domain evaluation on two non-CRC datasets - PanNuke (1185 images) and the Amgad 2019 (151 images) breast gland histopathology dataset. These datasets differ substantially from EBHI-Seg in organ type, staining characteristics, annotation protocol (nuclei-centric vs. gland-centric), and morphological structure. A strict zero-shot setting was employed, where the EBHI-Seg-trained MAC-Net model was tested without any fine-tuning. Under this configuration, MAC-Net achieved an average accuracy of 59.80%, Dice score of 34.46%, and IoU of 22.48% on the PanNuke datase, and 60.79% accuracy, 20.55% Dice, and 12.73% IoU on the Amgad breast gland dataset. Although these results are considerably lower than those obtained on EBHI-Seg and GlaS, they are expected given the large domain shift and task mismatch. The results indicate that MAC-Net can generalize reasonably within colorectal histopathology. While robust transfer to different organs or annotation paradigms remains challenging, it defines a direction for future research.
Interpretability and uncertainty analysis

Grad-CAM visualization and Monte Carlo Dropout-based uncertainty analysis were used to test the interpretability and reliability of MAC-Net predictions. The resulting Grad-CAM heatmaps were scaled and superimposed onto the original histopathological images to show where the model in question was paying attention to during the segmentation process, thus pointing to the fact that the model seems to be paying attention to areas that are relevant to biologically meaningful tissue structures in the sample of CRC. The approach minimizes the black-box aspects that are often attributed to the deep learning structure and contributes to the creation of a system of explainable AI (XAI). Figure 8 shows six representative images, one of each tumour type (Normal, Polyp, Low-grade IN, High-grade IN, Serrated Adenoma, and Adenocarcinoma) and the associated Grad-CAM mappings.
Grad-CAM visualizations for interpretability.

The strong activation is represented in red-colored areas in the heatmaps, and it relates to tumoral structures. The model is mostly focused on densely compacted glands in adenocarcinoma, distorted gland formations or mucosal protrusions in serrated adenoma and polyps, and irregular glandular architecture with nuclear atypia in low and high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia. These areas are highlighted in line with diagnostic patterns that are usually studied by pathologists, implying that the model focuses on patterns occurring at tissue levels that are consistent with clinically meaningful ones. This interpretability can be used to refine the systematic model, as well as potentially aid in more transparently assessing the model in the medical setting.

Computational complexity analysis

In order to determine the viability of investigating the implementation of MAC-Net within the resource-limited clinical environment, we calculated its computational efficiency. MAC-Net has 2.48 million trainable parameters (approximately 9.46 MB), which is quite lightweight in comparison with most of the current attention-driven or transformer-based networks used in segmentation. A layer-wise analytical FLOP estimation, based on multiply accumulate operations across all convolutional and dense layers, yields approximately 22.51 GFLOPs for a 256x256x3 input, reflecting a moderate computational load relative to the achieved accuracy. Empirical inference evaluation further demonstrated an average processing time of 0.6048 s per image on an NVIDIA T4 GPU in Google Colab (using a 20-image batch). In future studies, we aim to explore optimization strategies to reduce inference latency and enable real-time deployment on edge devices.

passages.text: A series of ablation experiments were conducted using the EBHI-Seg dataset to evaluate the individual and combined contributions of MAC-Net's core components. The evaluation began with a baseline U-Net encoder-decoder model, after which hierarchical feature extraction (H), attention refinement (A), and multi-scale contextual fusion (M) were introduced incrementally. Each module was individually tested in all the possible pairwise and complete combinations. Table 5 gives a summary of the performance of every variant.
Visual comparison of MAC-Net and its variants.

The findings suggest that adding any one of the individual modules (H, A, and M) to the baseline U-Net will result in a statistically significant segmentation improvement. Additional developments are seen when two modules are merged. The full architecture of MAC-Net that incorporates all three modules is the most accurate and can be used to justify its usefulness in the process of histopathological segmenting of the CRC on the EBHI-Seg dataset. In Fig. 10, the visual comparison between segmentation outputs of the baseline U-Net and its module-augmented counterparts is shown. All rows display the various stages of the CRC, and all columns indicate predictions of a specific model set-up. At all times, MAC-Net generates segmentation masks that are much closer to the ground truth with better localization of boundaries and better structural preservation, compared to its U-Net variants - particularly in complicated tissue areas.

The progressive improvement of each variant points to the robustness of the unified architecture of MAC-Net. With the hierarchical feature extraction, adaptive attention, and multi-scale contextual fusion, the model represents the detailed local information at the same time, preserving the higher-level structural context. This synergy helps to achieve more accurate gland segmentation at boundaries and enhances morphological continuity, where even the single-module variants are limited in the difficult tissue cases.
Discussion

The findings made in EBHI-Seg and GIaS prove that MAC-Net is able to segment the gland structures in colorectal glands correctly, particularly in samples with proper glandular borders. The hierarchical part of feature extraction, attention refinement, and multi-scale aggregation modules seems to be correlated in their operation to maintain continuity of structure and minimize fragmentation. This finding is supported by Ablation experiments, which demonstrate that the full model provides better performance than all the simplified variants and that the integration of modules together increases both the detailed boundary detection and the contextual reasoning.

Evaluation across external datasets gives information on the generalization of the models. MAC-Net retained high performance on EBHI-Seg and moderate performance on GIaS without retraining; the decrease in staining on PanNuke and Amgad demonstrates that the organ morphology, tissue characteristics, and staining variability affect segmentation performance. Such results suggest that MAC-Net is able to learn visual patterns on CRC better, yet it cannot be generalized to other types of datasets with various structural properties or nucleus-based attributes. This limitation could be overcome through the incorporation of multimodal data in the process of training, as they would offer a more diverse representation of features. The same behaviour was reported in earlier gland segmentation works, revealing that domain shift will continue to be a major obstacle to histopathological AI systems.

The uncertainty and interpretability studies help in the knowledge of model reliability. Grad-CAM images indicate that MAC-Net is focused on gland-rich and boundary-relevant figures, which are consistent with pathological decision features. The small uncertainty distribution indicates the confidence is constant in the majority of predictions, though the large uncertainty in the areas of complex stroma expresses that the model is less certain in the situations where the boundaries of the glands are ambiguous. These observances reinforce the importance of using the network as a decision-support tool alongside expert review rather than as a standalone diagnostic system.

In order to put MAC-Net perspectives into perspective, we relate its design to the latest trends in medical image segmentation. NHBS-Net, uses feature-fusion attention on neonatal hip ultrasound segmentation, which proves the capability of hierarchical representation combination to better segmentation in terms of boundary interpretation. Further, a dual-encoder provides an inter-view cross-attention of low- and high-magnification images to show both the global and fine-structure information of the tissue during the process of histopathological cancer analysis. MAC-Net adheres to the same architectural trend and integrates multi-scale representation, hierarchical context encoding, and attention-refined feature refinement into one end-to-end system, which, in our experiments, ensures the preservation of tissue boundaries and novel gland morphologies.

Even though MAC-Net is proposed and tested to work on the specific task of colorectal gland segmentation, the framework is domain-agnostic. Multi-scale feature aggregation helps the model to detect structural differences in the different resolutions, and contextual-attention fusion facilitates the isolation of meaningful and uninformative areas. These characteristics suggest potential flexibility to the other context of segmentation, like differentiating between true and reflective objects, which cannot be detected in a mirrorand selecting saliently structured information in low-density underwater images. Although these applications are outside the clinical scope of this paper, they show an encouraging trend in the direction of future research and suggest that the MAC-Net can be potentially applied to non-medical segmentation tasks, although additional validation of the hypothesis is required.

There are several limitations that should be acknowledged. The experiment relies on two colorectal datasets, which is a limitation to exposure to different tissue variability. The reduction in performance observed during domain shift underscores the importance of stain normalization, domain adaptation, and multi-institution assessment. The speed of processing is average, and unlike batch inference, it will need additional refinement to be deployed as a whole slide in real-time. Clinical validation by expert pathologists remains outstanding, and it is a critical action to be taken to achieve quality translational application.

On the whole, MAC-Net is effective in colorectal gland segmentation and may have a useful potential in the analysis of CRC glands. The enhanced stain robustness, cross-domain adaptation, and inference speed, as well as expert validation in the future, will make it more applicable. The further development of such aspects can facilitate the development towards reliable clinical integration and extension to other segmentation conditions other than colorectal tissue.
Conclusion and future work

This article introduced MAC-Net as a hybrid deep learning system that is used to segment colorectal cancer histopathological images. The combination of top-down feature extraction and bottom-up contextual refinement led to the model showing strong results on EBHI-Seg and promising results on GIaS, with deteriorating results in the presence of large domain variation. Grad-CAM and uncertainty mapping allowed gaining an insight into the behaviour of the prediction, underlining the areas that impact the model results and proving the cases when the prediction needs further inspection by specialists. Ablation experiments also affirmed that all the components played a significant role in the overall segmentation capacity. Combined, these findings indicate that MAC-Net could function as an interpretable and efficient component within digital pathology-assisted workflows, provided that further validation is undertaken.

The remaining challenges will be addressed in future research. Relatively lower results with transitional tissue classes indicate that domain-sensitive learning of features and multimodal indications that are more attentive to subtle morphological changes are required. Pruning, quantization, or lightweight architectural variants can be used to achieve efficiency and can be deployed faster on a clinical or resource-constrained system. Massive, inter-center validation and stain-diverse data will be necessary to guarantee high-quality generalizability between patient populations and imaging circumstances.

Overall, MAC-Net is ascertained to be an accurate, interpretable, and adaptable system in the reviewed field, which makes it a promising research basis in the field of CRC histopathological image analysis. Continuous work will consist of evaluating more organs, adding clinical metadata, and making the model oriented towards real-time diagnostic integration.

passages.text: Novel association between atherogenic index of plasma and bone mineral density in men: a retrospective analysis
Background
This study aimed to investigate the association between the atherogenic index of plasma (AIP), lipid parameters, and bone mineral density (BMD) in men with osteoporosis.
Methods

This retrospective, single-center study included 430 male patients aged >= 50 years admitted to the First Hospital of Shanxi Medical University between June 2022 and December 2024. Routine blood lipid profiles, including total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL) were collected. AIP was calculated as log10(TG/HDL). BMD was measured using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) and patients were categorized into normal (NO), osteopenia (ON), and osteoporosis (OP) groups. Correlation analysis, principal component analysis (PCA), and one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) were applied.
Results

Among 430 participants, 218 were classified as NO, 133 as ON, and 79 as OP. PCA revealed that the first two components (PC1 eigenvalue = 2.127, PC2 eigenvalue = 1.531) explained 73.15% of the total variance (PC1: 42.53%, PC2: 30.62%), with AIP and TC identified as major contributors to BMD variation. Correlation analysis showed that AIP (r = -0.26,p = 0.003), TG (r = -0.15,p = 0.047), and HDL (r = 0.34,p < 0.001) were significantly associated with BMD, while TC and LDL were not. ANOVA demonstrated significant group differences in AIP and HDL, particularly between the OP and NO groups.
Conclusion
Elevated AIP and altered HDL levels are associated with reduced BMD in men, highlighting their potential role in the early identification and risk stratification of male osteoporosis.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12902-025-02128-3.
Mini abstract

This study examined the association between blood lipids and bone mineral density (BMD) in men. Among 430 participants, BMD showed significant correlations with the atherogenic index of plasma (AIP, p = 0.003), triglycerides (TG, p = 0.047), and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL, p < 0.001). Elevated AIP and altered HDL levels were linked to lower BMD, suggesting these lipid markers may serve as cost-effective indicators for assessing osteoporosis risk in men.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12902-025-02128-3.
Introduction

Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder characterized by reduced bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration, leading to increased bone fragility and fracture risk. It is generally classified into two types: primary and secondary osteoporosis.Primary osteoporosis develops in the absence of other diseases, most commonly in postmenopausal women due to estrogen deficiency, and in elderly individuals as a consequence of age-related bone loss.

infons.name: Myotonia with Skeletal Abnormalities and Mental Retardation

passages.text: Although osteoporosis is often perceived as a women's disease, it also represents a major health concern in men. Approximately 20% of the 44 million Americans with osteoporosis or low bone density are men, who account for 30-40% of osteoporotic fractures. The lifetime fracture risk among men aged >= 50 years is estimated to range from 13% to 30%.Secondary osteoporosis, by contrast, arises from identifiable causes such as endocrine disorders (e.g., hyperthyroidism, hypercortisolism), chronic diseases (e.g., diabetes, chronic kidney disease, inflammatory bowel disease), or long-term glucocorticoid therapy.Epidemiological data suggest that secondary osteoporosis affects up to 30% of postmenopausal women, more than 50% of premenopausal women, and 50-80% of men. These observations highlight the substantial clinical and public health burden of osteoporosis in both sexes and underscore the importance of improved risk stratification and preventive strategies.

Certain underlying diseases associated with secondary osteoporosis, such as diabetes and chronic kidney disease, can alter lipid metabolism, contributing to bone loss. Diabetic patients often have dyslipidemia, with elevated triglycerides and reduced HDL, promoting inflammation and oxidative stress that worsen bone resorption. Similarly, chronic kidney disease leads to lipid disturbances, including increased LDL, further impairing bone metabolism. Understanding these lipid abnormalities can help identify high-risk individuals and guide prevention efforts.

This link between lipid metabolism and bone health is not only relevant in the context of secondary osteoporosis but also in primary osteoporosis.In recent years, AIP, defined as log10(TG/HDL), has emerged as a strong predictor of cardiovascular disease. AIP is associated with small dense LDL particles and increased cholesterol esterification rates, reflecting adverse lipid metabolism. Beyond its role in cardiovascular disease, AIP has been linked to trabecular bone microarchitecture deterioration, suggesting a potential interplay between lipid and bone metabolism.

Recent studies have further demonstrated that elevated AIP levels are independently associated with reduced bone mineral density and increased fracture risk in various populations, including postmenopausal women and individuals with metabolic disorders. Moreover, AIP has been linked to markers of oxidative stress and inflammation that promote osteoclast activation and impair osteoblast differentiation, suggesting a potential mechanistic pathway between dyslipidemia and bone loss.

Although research on AIP and osteoporosis has primarily focused on postmenopausal women, its relationship with bone health in men remains largely unexplored. Given the growing recognition of AIP as an indicator of bone quality and turnover, investigating this association in men could yield valuable insights into sex-specific pathophysiological mechanisms. Therefore, this study aimed to elucidate the associations between AIP, lipid parameters, and BMD in men, and to evaluate their potential predictive value for the early detection of osteoporosis.
Data and methods
Study population
Male patients aged >= 50 years admitted to the Department of Endocrinology, First Hospital of Shanxi Medical University, between June 2022 and December 2024 were retrospectively included.
Inclusion criteria and exclusion criteria
Inclusion criteria: (1) Male, ages >= 50years; (2)Diagnosis of osteoporosis according to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria.

Exclusion criteria: (1) Long-term use of drugs affecting bone metabolism (e.g., glucocorticoids, bisphosphonates, active vitamin D); (2) History of primary bone tumors or bone metastases; (3) Previous treatment for osteoporosis; (4) Endocrine disorders (e.g., hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism); (5) Chronic diseases (e.g., chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, metabolic syndrome, and diabetes).
BMD measurement and group division

BMD was measured using a Hologic Discovery Wi DXA system (Hologic Inc., Marlborough, MA, USA). The system underwent daily calibration and quality control (QC) with a manufacturer-provided phantom to ensure accuracy.For T-score calculation, we used the Hologic reference database for men. All BMD measurements were performed by experienced radiologic technologists who were blinded to the patients' clinical information. The lowest T-score from the lumbar spine was used to classify patients into three groups: NO (normal): T-score > -1.0;ON (osteopenia): -2.5 < T-score <= -1.0 OP (osteoporosis): T-score <= -2.5.

All lumbar spine DXA images were visually inspected for vertebral fractures, osteophytes, and abdominal aortic calcification. Scans with significant artifacts that could affect BMD measurements were excluded from the analysis.
Laboratory measurements and AIP calculation

Serum N-MID osteocalcin (bone Gla protein, BGP) was quantified using the Roche e601 N-MID osteocalcin assay, with an intra- and inter-assay coefficient of variation (CV) of 4.49% to ensure precision. All measurements were conducted under standardized conditions to minimize variation.

Serum lipid profiles, including TC, TG, HDL, and LDL, were measured using standard enzymatic methods on the Beckman AU5800. Calibration was performed every two weeks using certified reference materials to ensure accuracy. All lipid parameters were expressed in mmol/L.

Participants fasted for at least 12 h before blood collection to standardize measurements and reduce variability. Samples were collected in the morning to minimize diurnal variations, and analyses were completed within 2 h.
AIP calculation is described in the Introduction section. The study design and data analysis workflow are summarized in Fig. 1.
Flow chart
Statistical analysis

The normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test, and the homogeneity of variances was evaluated using Levene's test. Variables with a normal distribution were expressed as mean +- standard deviation (SD), while those with a non-normal distribution were presented as median (interquartile range, IQR). Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages.

Between-group differences were analyzed using ANOVA, followed by the Bonferroni post hoc test for multiple comparisons. Post-hoc Bonferroni comparisons of clinical and biochemical parameters among the three groups are presented in Table S1. Nonparametric tests (such as the Kruskal-Wallis test) were applied for variables that did not meet the assumptions of normality or homogeneity of variances.

Regression Analysis: To assess the relationship between AIP and BMD, multivariate linear regression analyses were performed (Table S2). Model 1 was unadjusted; Model 2 adjusted for age and Body Mass Index (BMI); and Model 3 further adjusted for platelet count, systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 (25(OH)D), N-MID osteocalcin, beta-Collagen Degradation Products (beta-CTX), and Procollagen Type I N-Terminal Propeptide (PINP). Regression coefficients (B), standard errors (SE), and standardized beta coefficients (beta) were reported, with stepwise regression used to evaluate independent associations between variables.

Ordinal Logistic Regression: Additionally, ordinal logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between AIP and BMD categories (normal, osteopenia, osteoporosis). Variables included in the model were AIP, age, BMI, platelet count, SBP, DBP, 25(OH)D, N-MID osteocalcin, beta-CTX, and PINP (Table S3). Estimated coefficients (B), standard errors (SE), Wald statistics, p-values, and odds ratios (Exp(B)) were reported.

PCA was conducted to identify the most influential lipid-related variables associated with BMD. PCA was performed using varimax orthogonal rotation to facilitate the interpretation of component loadings. Components with eigenvalues greater than 1 (PC1 and PC2) were retained for further analysis. As PCA is an exploratory multivariate technique that does not involve hypothesis testing of pairwise correlations, correlation coefficients (r), p-values, or 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were not provided, as these are not typically reported in this type of analysis.

Correlation Analysis: Pearson correlation analysis was employed to examine associations between AIP, lipid parameters, and BMD (Fig. 1). Table 2 presents the correlation between the Atherogenic Index and male osteoporosis. All statistical tests were two-tailed, with a p-value of < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic performance of various variables in distinguishing different BMD status groups (normal, osteopenia, and osteoporosis). Figure S1 shows the ROC curves, and Table S4 provides a summary of the ROC analysis, including the area under the curve(AUC), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), cut-off values, sensitivity, and specificity. The AUC and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated and reported to evaluate the discriminative ability of each variable.

Although a formal power analysis was not conducted, the total sample size of 430 participants was deemed adequate based on previous studies with similar designs and effect sizes, ensuring sufficient statistical power to detect moderate group differences.
Results
General characteristics

A total of 430 male participants were included: 218 in the NO group, 133 in the ON group, and 79 in the OP group. The mean ages were comparable among the groups (NO: 63.62 +- 8.16; ON: 63.02 +- 7.32; OP: 63.61 +- 8.28 years). Significant between-group differences were observed in BMI, platelet count, alanine aminotransferase (ALT)(P = 0.003), Indirect bilirubin (IBIL)(P = 0.007), alkaline phosphatase (ALP)(P = 0.016), HDL (P = 0.000), beta-CTX (P = 0.025), and N-MID osteocalcin (p = 0.015). Other baseline parameters, including age, SBP, DBP, pulse rate, lymphocyte count, neutrophil count, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), total protein, globulin, albumin, TBIL, DBIL (Direct Bilirubin), TC, LDL, serum calcium (Ca), serum magnesium (Mg), urea, uric acid (UA), serum phosphorus (P), 25(OH)D; PINP and parathyroid hormone (PTH) did not differ significantly(Table 1).These baseline differences, particularly in BMI and ALT levels, may reflect overall health status and potentially influence bone metabolism and bone health.Post-hoc Bonferroni tests revealed significant differences among the three groups for weight, height, BMI, platelet count, AST, ALP, AIP, HDL, and N-MID osteocalcin (p < 0.05). Full post-hoc comparison results are provided in Supplementary Table S1.

Principal component analysis

PCA was applied to the five lipid-related variables (AIP, TC, TG, HDL and LDL) to reduce multicollinearity and identify independent lipid patterns associated with BMD. The analysis employed a varimax orthogonal rotation to enhance interpretability.

Two principal components with eigenvalues greater than 1 were extracted according to the Kaiser criterion: PC1 (eigenvalue = 2.127, variance contribution = 42.53%) and PC2 (eigenvalue = 1.531, variance contribution = 30.62%), together explaining 73.15% of the total variance. Among these variables, AIP and TC showed the highest loadings on PC1, indicating their dominant contribution to the lipid pattern related to BMD. The scree plot confirmed that the first two components accounted for most of the explained variance, and the score plots demonstrated a clear separation trend among groups along PC1 (Fig. 2).

Correlation between atherogenic index and male osteoporosis

Pearson correlation analysis demonstrated significant associations between AIP (p = 0.003), TG (p = 0.047), and HDL (p < 0.001) with the lowest BMD T-score, whereas TC (p = 0.418) and LDL (p = 0.373) showed no significant correlations (Table 2). Significance was denoted by "*" for p < 0.05 and "ns" for non-significant results. Interestingly, the lack of association for TC and LDL is clinically relevant, as previous studies have suggested potential links between lipid metabolism and bone health. Our findings indicate that TC/LDL levels may not serve as reliable indicators of osteoporosis risk in men, underscoring the greater importance of parameters such as AIP and HDL in reflecting lipid-related mechanisms of bone loss.

Additionally, BMI was positively correlated with weight (r = 0.86, p < 0.001) and negatively correlated with HDL (r = - 0.21, p < 0.05). Platelet count showed a moderate positive correlation with AST (r = 0.34, p < 0.05), suggesting potential metabolic and hepatic interactions influencing bone health.
Regression analysis results

To further explore the relationships between lipid markers and bone mineral density, we performed multivariate linear regression analysis (Table S2). In Model 1 (unadjusted), AIP was significantly associated with the lowest T-score (B = 0.756, p = 0.006). However, in Model 2, after adjusting for age and BMI, AIP's effect diminished (B = 0.276, p = 0.323), and further adjustment for additional variables in Model 3 showed no significant association (B = 0.280, p = 0.325). These results indicate that while AIP may be related to BMD in an unadjusted model, the relationship weakens after accounting for confounding factors such as age and BMI.

Additionally, ordinal logistic regression analysis (Table S3) was conducted to assess the association of AIP with different BMD categories. AIP did not show a significant relationship with BMD categories (Exp(B) = 0.856, p = 0.670), suggesting that other variables, particularly BMI, may be more predictive of BMD classification.
Between-group comparison
Based on the PCA and correlation findings, one-way ANOVA was performed to further assess differences in lipid-related markers across the three BMD groups. The analysis revealed:

AIP: significantly higher in the OP group compared with the NO group (p = 0.013), but no significant differences between ON and the other groups.HDL: significantly higher in the OP group compared with both NO and ON groups (p < 0.001).TC, TG, and LDL: no significant differences among the three groups (all p > 0.05)(Fig. 3). Consistent with the correlation analysis, the absence of group differences in TC and LDL further supports the interpretation that these conventional lipid markers may have limited relevance in male osteoporosis, in contrast to the stronger and more consistent associations observed for AIP and HDL(Fig. 3).

ROC curve analysis

ROC analysis was conducted to evaluate the diagnostic performance of various lipid-related parameters. Figure S1 illustrates the ROC curves for AIP, HDL, and other lipid parameters, while Table S4 provides a detailed summary of the ROC analysis, including AUC, 95% confidence intervals (CIs), cut-off values, sensitivity, and specificity. The AUC values indicate the discriminative ability of each variable in distinguishing different BMD status groups.
Discussion
Research background and summary of results

Compared to postmenopausal osteoporosis, male osteoporosis remains largely underdiagnosed and undertreated due to lower screening frequency and controversies surrounding BMD testing standards. Our study aims to explore the role of atherosclerosis-related biomarkers in male osteoporosis. We found that biomarkers related to atherosclerosis are significantly associated with decreased BMD, suggesting they may be involved in the pathophysiological processes of male osteoporosis. The economic burden of osteoporosis is significant, with fractures costing $37.5 billion in Europe in 2017, and projected to rise to $47.4 billion by 2030, particularly due to hip fractures, which account for the largest share of costs (57%).
Association between AIP and osteoporosis

Our findings align with previous studies indicating a non-linear association between AIP and BMD, with sex and age potentially modifying this relationship. While HDL-BMD associations remain inconsistent:sometimes positive, negative, or U-shaped, especially among males :research specific to men is limited. This highlights the need for further studies to validate these findings. Our study provides novel evidence linking atherosclerosis-related biomarkers, particularly AIP, to male osteoporosis, a topic previously focused primarily on postmenopausal women.
Mechanism discussion

Consistent with our hypothesis, AIP was significantly higher in the osteoporosis group than in the normal BMD group, suggesting that lipid-related markers may contribute to the pathophysiological processes underlying bone loss in men. Notably, principal component analysis revealed that AIP and TC were the most influential lipid variables, indicating they may serve as more comprehensive risk assessment tools than individual lipid markers.

Dyslipidemia may affect bone metabolism through inflammation-oxidative stress pathways that enhance osteoclastogenesis and impair osteoblast function. HDL provides antioxidative and anti-inflammatory protection, while oxidized LDL promotes RANKL(Receptor Activator of Nuclear Factor-kappaB Ligand) expression and bone resorption, further contributing to bone loss. This interpretation aligns with evidence linking lipid toxicity, marrow adiposity, and Wnt(Wingless/Integrated signaling pathway)/PPARgamma(Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor Gamma) signaling to skeletal health.
